clue: Muslims mark the end of the Hajj pilgrimage with prayers, new clothes and shared meat
description: The Festival of Sacrifice honours Abraham's devotion to God. It falls on 10 Dhu al-Hijjah, expected on Sunday 16 May in 2027, though moon sighting can shift it by a day.
fact: Sacrificial meat is traditionally split in three: a third for the family, a third for friends and neighbours, and a third for people in need.

clue: Norwegian children parade with flags to celebrate the founding law signed in 1814
description: Norway celebrates the signing of its constitution at Eidsvoll on 17 May 1814 with children's parades, brass bands, national costumes and lots of ice cream.
fact: Unlike most national days, the highlight is a children's parade rather than a military one; in Oslo the royal family waves from the palace balcony.

clue: Galleries and collections around the globe open their doors, often for free
description: International Museum Day has been organised every 18 May since 1977 by the International Council of Museums (ICOM) to show how museums matter to society.
fact: Each year has its own theme, and many museums stretch the day into a "Night of Museums" with late opening hours.

clue: Turkey marks Ataturk's 1919 landing at Samsun with stadium shows by young people
description: Commemoration of Ataturk, Youth and Sports Day recalls 19 May 1919, when Mustafa Kemal landed in Samsun to begin the national movement. He dedicated the day to the nation's young.
fact: Ataturk's real birth date was never recorded, so he chose 19 May as his symbolic birthday.

clue: Buddhists honour the birth, enlightenment and passing of the Buddha at a full moon
description: Vesak, the UN-recognised Day of Vesak, is held on the full moon of May, which falls on 20 May in 2027. Some countries use local lunar calendars and celebrate on other days.
fact: The UN General Assembly recognised the Day of Vesak in 1999; lanterns, temple visits and acts of charity mark the day.

clue: Lindbergh landed at Le Bourget after the first solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic
description: On 21 May 1927 Charles Lindbergh landed near Paris in his plane after 33.5 hours alone over the Atlantic. 2027 marks the centenary of the flight.
fact: The plane had no front window: an extra fuel tank blocked the view, so Lindbergh looked ahead with a periscope or by leaning out the side.

clue: Arthur Conan Doyle's birthday honours his pipe-smoking Baker Street detective
description: Fans of the great detective celebrate on 22 May, the birthday of his creator Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, born in Edinburgh in 1859.
fact: The line "Elementary, my dear Watson" never appears in any of Conan Doyle's original stories.

clue: Swedish botanist born in 1707 who gave every species a two-part Latin name
description: Carl Linnaeus, father of modern taxonomy, was born on 23 May 1707 in Rashult, Sweden. His binomial naming system, like Homo sapiens, is still used today.
fact: His book Species Plantarum (1753) is the official starting point for the scientific names of plants.

clue: Canada's Monday holiday before 25 May honours a 19th-century queen's birthday
description: Victoria Day falls on the last Monday before 25 May, which is 24 May in 2027. It honours Queen Victoria's birthday and unofficially opens summer in Canada.
fact: Canadians nickname it "May Two-Four", a pun on the date and on a case of 24 beers.

clue: Marks the 1963 founding of the continent's unity organisation in Addis Ababa
description: The continent celebrates the founding of the Organisation of African Unity on 25 May 1963, today's African Union, with concerts, food and cultural events.
fact: The OAU was founded by 32 newly independent states; the African Union that replaced it in 2002 now has 55 members.

clue: Irish writer Bram Stoker's novel about a Transylvanian count appeared in 1897
description: Bram Stoker's vampire novel was first published in London on 26 May 1897, which is why fans celebrate the date as World Dracula Day.
fact: Stoker never visited Transylvania; he researched the setting in libraries and travel books.

clue: Catholic feast with street processions and flower carpets, 60 days after Easter
description: The Feast of the Body and Blood of Christ falls on the Thursday 60 days after Easter: 27 May in 2027, as Easter is 28 March. Some countries move it to the Sunday.
fact: In towns such as Sitges in Spain, streets are covered with carpets of flower petals for the procession to walk over.

clue: Australian pop star born in Melbourne in 1968, singer of Can't Get You Out of My Head
description: The Australian singer, one of the best-selling female artists of all time, was born in Melbourne on 28 May 1968.
fact: She first became famous playing the mechanic Charlene in the TV soap opera Neighbours.

clue: Nepal honours Hillary and Tenzing's 1953 first ascent of the world's highest peak
description: International Everest Day, declared by Nepal in 2008, marks 29 May 1953, when Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first reached the summit at 8,849 m.
fact: Hillary photographed Tenzing on the summit, but there is no clear photo of Hillary himself at the top.

clue: Spain's Atlantic archipelago marks its first regional parliament session of 1983
description: Dia de Canarias on 30 May marks the first session of the Canary Islands Parliament in 1983, celebrated with folk music, traditional dress and local food.
fact: The islands were named after dogs (Latin canis), not birds; the canary bird was later named after the islands.

clue: The Great Clock in the Westminster tower first started keeping time in 1859
description: The Great Clock of the Palace of Westminster started on 31 May 1859. Its giant bell, popularly called by this name, began striking the hours that July.
fact: The tower that houses it was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012 for Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee.

clue: Kenya marks the 1963 start of self-government, a step before full independence
description: Kenya's public holiday on 1 June marks the day in 1963 when the country gained internal self-rule from Britain.
fact: Madaraka is the Swahili word for "authority" or "self-rule".

clue: Italians voted in 1946 to abolish the monarchy; Rome celebrates with a parade
description: Festa della Repubblica marks the referendum of 2-3 June 1946, in which Italians chose a republic over the monarchy. Rome hosts a parade along Via dei Fori Imperiali.
fact: The Frecce Tricolori aerobatic jets trail green, white and red smoke over Rome during the celebration.

clue: UN observance for two-wheeled, pedal-powered transport, adopted in 2018
description: The UN General Assembly declared 3 June World Bicycle Day in 2018 to celebrate a simple, affordable, clean way to get around.
fact: The ancestor of the bike, Karl Drais's pedal-less "running machine", was built in Germany in 1817.

clue: Salvation Army volunteers served fried rings of dough to US soldiers in World War I
description: National Donut Day falls on the first Friday of June (4 June in 2027). The Salvation Army created it in 1938 to honour volunteers who served doughnuts to troops.
fact: The volunteers who fried them near the front lines in France were nicknamed "Donut Lassies".

clue: Danes mark their 1849 constitution with political speeches and picnics
description: Denmark's Constitution Day celebrates the constitution of 5 June 1849, which made the country a constitutional monarchy. Politicians give speeches at outdoor gatherings.
fact: The same date is also Father's Day in Denmark.

clue: 1 Muharram opens 1449 AH, counted from the Prophet's journey to Medina
description: Islamic New Year marks 1 Muharram. In 2027 the year 1449 AH is expected to begin on 6 June, subject to local moon sighting.
fact: The Hijri calendar counts from the Prophet Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

clue: The world's smallest state became sovereign when Italy ratified the Lateran Treaty
description: The Lateran Treaty between Italy and the Holy See was ratified on 7 June 1929, creating an independent state inside Rome under the pope.
fact: At about 44 hectares, it is the smallest country in the world by both area and population.

clue: UN observance for the seas that cover about 71 percent of the planet's surface
description: Proposed at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio and recognised by the UN in 2008, the day on 8 June celebrates the seas and the life within them.
fact: Scientists estimate that about half of the oxygen we breathe is produced by tiny ocean plankton.

clue: Crews paddle to drumbeats and eat sticky rice dumplings in memory of poet Qu Yuan
description: Duanwu falls on the 5th day of the 5th lunar month, which is 9 June in 2027. Crews race to drumbeats and families eat zongzi.
fact: Legend says people threw rice into the river so the fish would eat it instead of the drowned poet Qu Yuan.

clue: Lisbon honours national poet Luis de Camoes, author of The Lusiads
description: Dia de Portugal, de Camoes e das Comunidades Portuguesas is held on 10 June, the date Camoes died in 1580, and celebrates Portuguese communities worldwide.
fact: Camoes's epic The Lusiads (1572) tells of Vasco da Gama's voyage to India; legend says he saved the manuscript from a shipwreck.

clue: French ocean explorer born in 1910 who co-invented the Aqua-Lung
description: The French naval officer, filmmaker and ocean explorer was born on 11 June 1910 in Saint-Andre-de-Cubzac.
fact: His underwater film The Silent World won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 1956.

clue: Brazilian couples swap gifts on the eve of Saint Anthony, the matchmaker saint
description: Brazil's lovers' day is celebrated on 12 June instead of 14 February, on the eve of the feast of Saint Anthony, who is known as a matchmaker.
fact: The date was promoted in 1949 by an advertising executive to boost sales in June, a slow month for shops.

clue: Launched in 1972, this NASA probe was the first to pass the orbit of Neptune in 1983
description: On 13 June 1983 Pioneer 10 crossed the orbit of Neptune, becoming the first human-made object to travel beyond the planets of the Solar System.
fact: It carries a gold-anodised plaque showing a man, a woman and the Sun's location, in case aliens ever find it.

clue: Americans honour the Stars and Stripes, adopted by Congress in 1777
description: On 14 June 1777 the Second Continental Congress adopted the first official US flag. President Wilson proclaimed the national observance in 1916.
fact: The current 50-star design has been in use since 4 July 1960, longer than any earlier version.

clue: King John sealed this charter at Runnymede in 1215, limiting royal power
description: On 15 June 1215 King John agreed to the "Great Charter" at Runnymede, near Windsor. It became a symbol of the idea that no one is above the law.
fact: Only four original copies of the 1215 charter survive: two at the British Library and one each in Lincoln and Salisbury.

clue: Dubliners in Edwardian dress retrace a single day from James Joyce's novel Ulysses
description: Ulysses takes place on 16 June 1904, following Leopold Bloom through Dublin. Fans celebrate with readings, costumes and Gorgonzola sandwiches.
fact: Joyce chose 16 June 1904 because it is said to be the day of his first date with Nora Barnacle, his future wife.

clue: Reykjavik celebrates the 1944 founding of its republic with parades and sweets
description: The North Atlantic island became an independent republic on 17 June 1944. The day is celebrated with parades, music and a woman dressed as the "Mountain Woman".
fact: The date was chosen because it is the birthday of independence hero Jon Sigurdsson, born in 1811.

clue: Liverpool-born Beatle who wrote Yesterday and Hey Jude, born in 1942
description: The Beatles' bassist and songwriter was born in Liverpool on 18 June 1942, and turns 85 in 2027.
fact: Guinness World Records has named him the most successful composer and recording artist in popular music history.

clue: US federal holiday marking the 1865 news of freedom reaching enslaved Texans
description: On 19 June 1865 Union troops in Galveston announced that enslaved people in Texas were free. The day is celebrated with parades, cookouts and readings.
fact: Its name blends "June" and "nineteenth"; it became a US federal holiday in 2021.

clue: Dads get cards and ties on the third Sunday of June in the US, UK and Canada
description: Many countries honour fathers on the third Sunday of June, which is 20 June in 2027. Others, such as Germany and Australia, use different dates.
fact: Sonora Smart Dodd organised the first one in Spokane, Washington, in 1910, inspired by her widowed father who raised six children.

clue: UN observance on the solstice, proposed by India's prime minister in 2014
description: The International Day of Yoga is held on 21 June, the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere. Millions join mass sessions in parks and squares.
fact: The first edition in 2015 set a Guinness record when about 35,985 people practised together in New Delhi.

clue: Maradona's handball goal against England at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico City
description: On 22 June 1986 Diego Maradona punched the ball past England's goalkeeper in a World Cup quarter-final; he credited it to "the hand of God".
fact: Four minutes later he scored the "Goal of the Century", dribbling past half the English team.

clue: Somerset farm festival with a Pyramid Stage returns after a fallow year
description: The famous music festival at Worthy Farm opens on Wednesday 23 June and runs to 27 June 2027, returning after its 2026 rest year.
fact: Tickets for the first festival in 1970 cost one pound and included free milk from the farm.

clue: Cusco re-enacts the Inca Festival of the Sun at the fortress of Sacsayhuaman
description: The Inca winter-solstice festival honoured the sun god Inti. Since 1944 Cusco has staged a grand re-enactment every 24 June.
fact: Spanish authorities banned the festival in the 16th century; the modern revival draws thousands of spectators.

clue: Swedes dance around a flowered maypole and eat pickled herring with new potatoes
description: Swedish Midsummer Eve falls on the Friday between 19 and 25 June, which is 25 June in 2027. It is one of the biggest celebrations of the Swedish year.
fact: Tradition says that if you sleep with seven kinds of wild flowers under your pillow, you will dream of your future spouse.

clue: Bloomsbury published a boy wizard's first adventure in 1997, with 500 hardbacks
description: The Philosopher's Stone was published in the UK on 26 June 1997, so 2027 marks 30 years of the boy wizard.
fact: Twelve publishers rejected J.K. Rowling's manuscript before Bloomsbury took it on.

clue: Barclays installed the first one in Enfield in 1967; it paid out against paper vouchers
description: The world's first ATM opened at a Barclays branch in Enfield, north London, on 27 June 1967. 2027 is its 60th anniversary.
fact: Inventor John Shepherd-Barron wanted a six-digit PIN, but chose four because his wife could only remember four numbers.

clue: Math fans celebrate 6.28, twice the famous circle constant 3.14
description: Held on 28 June (6/28), this day celebrates the constant 6.283..., the ratio of a circle's circumference to its radius.
fact: Supporters argue it is more natural than pi because one full turn of a circle is exactly this many radians.

clue: Antoine de Saint-Exupery, born in 1900, wrote this tale of a boy from asteroid B-612
description: The French aviator and author of the beloved novella was born in Lyon on 29 June 1900.
fact: Saint-Exupery illustrated the book himself with his own watercolours.

clue: Recalls the 1908 Tunguska blast, which flattened a vast Siberian forest
description: The UN's International Asteroid Day on 30 June marks the 1908 Tunguska event and raises awareness of space rocks and planetary defence.
fact: The day was co-founded in 2014 by Queen guitarist and astrophysicist Brian May.

clue: Celebrates Confederation in 1867 with fireworks and red-and-white maple leaves
description: Canada Day marks 1 July 1867, when three colonies united as a single country under the British North America Act.
fact: Until 1982 the holiday was officially called Dominion Day.

clue: Cycling's greatest race starts at Edinburgh Castle, its first ever visit to Scotland
description: The 2027 edition of the famous bike race starts in Edinburgh on Friday 2 July with a British Grand Depart, before heading to Paris for 25 July.
fact: The leader wears a yellow jersey because the race's founding newspaper, L'Auto, was printed on yellow paper.

clue: Prague writer born in 1883 who imagined a man waking up as a giant insect
description: The author of The Metamorphosis and The Trial was born in Prague on 3 July 1883. His name gave us the adjective "Kafkaesque".
fact: Kafka asked his friend Max Brod to burn his manuscripts; Brod refused and published them instead.

clue: Americans mark the 1776 Declaration with fireworks, parades and barbecues
description: The US celebrates the adoption of the Declaration of Independence by the Continental Congress on 4 July 1776.
fact: Although adopted on 4 July, most delegates actually signed the Declaration on 2 August 1776.

clue: Louis Reard unveiled this daring two-piece swimsuit at a Paris pool in 1946
description: French engineer Louis Reard presented his two-piece swimsuit at the Piscine Molitor in Paris on 5 July 1946.
fact: It was named after a Pacific atoll where nuclear tests had begun days earlier, hoping it would cause an "explosive" reaction.

clue: A rocket at noon launches Pamplona's week of bull runs, red scarves and white clothes
description: The festival in Pamplona, Navarre, starts with the chupinazo rocket at noon on 6 July and continues until 14 July with daily bull runs.
fact: Ernest Hemingway made it world-famous in his 1926 novel The Sun Also Rises.

clue: Japanese star festival where wishes on paper strips are tied to bamboo branches
description: The festival on 7 July celebrates the yearly meeting of two lovers separated by the Milky Way, who may meet only on this night.
fact: The lovers Orihime and Hikoboshi are the stars Vega and Altair.

clue: German count born in 1838 whose name became a word for rigid airships
description: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, pioneer of rigid airships, was born in Konstanz on 8 July 1838.
fact: His first airship, LZ 1, made its first flight over Lake Constance in July 1900.

clue: The first lawn tennis championships began at the All England Club in 1877
description: The first Championships began on 9 July 1877. Exactly 150 years later, the 2027 tournament (28 June to 11 July) is in its second week.
fact: In 1877 there was only one event, the men's singles, with 22 players.

clue: Inventor of alternating-current systems, born in 1856 in Smiljan
description: The inventor and engineer was born on 10 July 1856 in Smiljan, in present-day Croatia. His work made modern electricity supply possible.
fact: The SI unit of magnetic flux density, the tesla, is named after him.

clue: Mongolia's summer festival of wrestling, horse racing and archery opens on 11 July
description: The national festival in Mongolia runs from 11 to 13 July, opening with a ceremony in Ulaanbaatar and the "three games of men".
fact: UNESCO added it to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2010; its horse races are ridden by child jockeys.

clue: UN observance on the birthday of the youngest Nobel Peace Prize winner
description: The UN marks Malala Yousafzai's birthday on 12 July to promote education for every girl and boy.
fact: She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014, aged just 17.

clue: Concerts at Wembley and Philadelphia in 1985 raised money for famine relief
description: The charity concerts on 13 July 1985 in London and Philadelphia were watched by an estimated 1.9 billion people.
fact: Queen's 21-minute set is often voted the greatest live performance in rock history.

clue: France's national holiday with a military parade on the Champs-Elysees
description: France's national day commemorates the storming of the prison-fortress in Paris on 14 July 1789, which began the French Revolution.
fact: The French simply call it "le 14 juillet"; officially it also celebrates the 1790 Festival of the Federation.

clue: Dutch master of light and shadow, born in Leiden in 1606, painted The Night Watch
description: The great painter of the Dutch Golden Age was born in Leiden on 15 July 1606.
fact: He created dozens of self-portraits over 40 years, recording himself from young man to old age.

clue: J.D. Salinger's 1951 novel narrated by teenager Holden Caulfield
description: Salinger's coming-of-age novel was published on 16 July 1951 and became a symbol of teenage rebellion.
fact: Salinger never allowed the novel to be made into a film.

clue: Kyoto's month-long July festival peaks with a parade of giant wooden floats
description: Kyoto's famous festival lasts all July; its highlight is the Yamaboko Junko procession of huge floats on 17 July.
fact: It began in 869 as a ritual to appease the gods during an epidemic.

clue: People give 67 minutes of service, one for each year of Madiba's public life
description: The UN marks Nelson Mandela's birthday, 18 July (1918), by asking people to spend 67 minutes helping others.
fact: The UN declared the day in 2009; it was first held while Mandela was still alive.

clue: French painter of ballet dancers, born in Paris in 1834
description: Edgar Degas, famous for his paintings and sculptures of dancers, was born in Paris on 19 July 1834.
fact: His wax sculpture Little Dancer Aged Fourteen wore a real bodice, tutu and hair ribbon.

clue: Armstrong and Aldrin stepped onto the Sea of Tranquility in 1969
description: On 20 July 1969 Apollo 11's lunar module Eagle touched down, and Neil Armstrong took "one small step" a few hours later.
fact: With no wind or rain up there, the astronauts' bootprints could last for millions of years.

clue: Brussels marks Leopold I's 1831 oath as first king with a parade and fireworks
description: Belgium's national day recalls 21 July 1831, when Leopold I swore allegiance to the constitution as the country's first king.
fact: The country has three official languages: Dutch, French and German.

clue: Her feast honours the follower who, the Gospels say, first saw the risen Jesus
description: Christians honour her on 22 July. In the Gospels she is the first witness to the empty tomb on Easter morning.
fact: Pope Francis raised her memorial to a full feast in 2016, calling her the "Apostle of the Apostles".

clue: Ethiopia's last emperor, born in 1892, revered as a messiah in Rastafari
description: The emperor of Ethiopia was born on 23 July 1892. His birthday is a holy day for followers of the Rastafari movement.
fact: Rastafari takes its name from his pre-coronation title, Ras Tafari Makonnen.

clue: Born in Caracas in 1783, The Liberator led much of South America to independence
description: The Venezuelan leader was born in Caracas on 24 July 1783; his birthday is a public holiday in Venezuela.
fact: The country of Bolivia is named after him.

clue: Rio's Maracana stadium hosts the final of the 2027 football tournament
description: Brazil hosts the 2027 FIFA tournament from 24 June to 25 July, with the final at the Maracana in Rio de Janeiro.
fact: It is the first edition held in South America.

clue: Swiss psychiatrist born in 1875 who coined "introvert" and "archetype"
description: The founder of analytical psychology was born in Kesswil, Switzerland, on 26 July 1875.
fact: He popularised terms like introvert, extravert and collective unconscious.

clue: "What's up, Doc?" The carrot-chewing cartoon rabbit debuted in A Wild Hare in 1940
description: Warner Bros.' wisecracking rabbit made his official debut in the cartoon A Wild Hare, released on 27 July 1940.
fact: He received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1985.

clue: Peru celebrates San Martin's 1821 declaration of independence in Lima
description: Peru's national holidays on 28 and 29 July mark Jose de San Martin's proclamation of independence in Lima on 28 July 1821.
fact: Peruvians are expected to fly the national flag outside their homes throughout July.

clue: Eisenhower signed the act creating America's civilian space agency in 1958
description: President Eisenhower signed the National Aeronautics and Space Act on 29 July 1958; the agency opened that October.
fact: It took over an older agency, NACA, and started with about 8,000 employees.

clue: UN observance for pals and companions, first proposed in Paraguay in 1958
description: The UN proclaimed 30 July the International Day of Friendship in 2011; the idea goes back to a 1958 proposal in Paraguay.
fact: In India and some other countries it is celebrated on the first Sunday of August with friendship bands.

clue: Apollo 15 astronauts first drove this electric car on the Moon in 1971
description: On 31 July 1971 Dave Scott and Jim Irwin took the first drive on the Moon in a battery-powered buggy.
fact: Three of the cars were used, and all three are still parked on the Moon.

clue: Bonfires and fireworks recall the 1291 alliance of three Alpine cantons
description: Switzerland's national day on 1 August recalls the Federal Charter of 1291, an alliance between Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.
fact: It only became a nationwide public holiday in 1994, after a popular vote.

clue: Barbados's summer festival climaxes with the Grand Kadooment costume parade
description: The Barbadian festival ends on Kadooment Day, the first Monday of August, which is 2 August in 2027.
fact: It began in the 1780s to celebrate the end of the sugar cane harvest.

clue: Set sail from Palos in 1492 with three ships, seeking a westward route to Asia
description: On 3 August 1492 the Genoese navigator left Palos de la Frontera, Spain, with the Nina, Pinta and Santa Maria.
fact: The Santa Maria ran aground off Hispaniola on Christmas Day 1492 and was abandoned.

clue: New Orleans trumpeter nicknamed Satchmo, singer of What a Wonderful World
description: The jazz legend was born in New Orleans on 4 August 1901.
fact: For most of his life he claimed he was born on 4 July 1900; a baptism record later revealed the real date.

clue: In 1888 she drove her husband's motorwagen 106 km to Pforzheim without telling him
description: In early August 1888 Bertha Benz made the first long-distance car journey, from Mannheim to Pforzheim, proving the automobile was practical.
fact: She bought fuel at a pharmacy in Wiesloch, now called the world's first filling station.

clue: The Scottish capital's August arts festival, the world's largest, opens its 80th edition
description: The world's biggest arts festival runs from 6 to 30 August 2027, filling Edinburgh with comedy, theatre and street shows.
fact: It began in 1947, when eight theatre groups turned up uninvited to the new Edinburgh International Festival.

clue: Felix Houphouet-Boigny led this West African nation out of French rule in 1960
description: Cote d'Ivoire celebrates its independence from France, proclaimed on 7 August 1960, with parades in Abidjan and Yamoussoukro.
fact: The country is the world's largest producer of cocoa beans.

clue: Chinese lovers' day when a weaver girl and a cowherd meet on a bridge of magpies
description: This festival falls on the 7th day of the 7th lunar month, 8 August in 2027. It is often called Chinese Valentine's Day.
fact: Girls traditionally prayed for skill at weaving and needlework on this night.

clue: The city-state marks its 1965 independence with a parade and fighter jets
description: The island republic became independent on 9 August 1965. The National Day Parade features flypasts, fireworks and a huge flag.
fact: It is one of only three surviving city-states, alongside Monaco and Vatican City.

clue: Paris royal palace that opened to the public as a museum in 1793
description: The former royal palace opened as a public museum on 10 August 1793, during the French Revolution.
fact: It is the world's most-visited museum, with nearly 9 million visitors in 2024.

clue: DJ Kool Herc's 1973 Bronx back-to-school party is seen as the genre's birth
description: On 11 August 1973 DJ Kool Herc played at a party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, looping drum breaks for dancers.
fact: For the 50th anniversary in 2023, the US Senate named 11 August Hip Hop Celebration Day.

clue: Honours the largest land animals; co-founded with Thailand in 2012
description: Since 2012 the 12 August day has raised awareness of threats to Asian and African elephants, such as poaching and habitat loss.
fact: An elephant's trunk contains around 40,000 muscles.

clue: Japanese ancestral spirits return home; families dance and float lanterns
description: This Buddhist festival honours ancestors' spirits. In most of Japan it is held from 13 to 16 August, with lanterns, grave visits and folk dancing.
fact: Tokushima's Awa Odori dance festival during this season attracts more than a million spectators.

clue: Muslims mark the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad on 12 Rabi al-Awwal
description: Mawlid an-Nabi is expected on 14 August 2027 (12 Rabi al-Awwal 1449), though moon sighting may vary it by a day.
fact: In Egypt, sweet shops sell colourful sugar dolls and horses especially for the occasion.

clue: Italy's mid-August holiday, when cities empty out and everyone heads for the beach
description: This Italian holiday on 15 August coincides with the Assumption of Mary; many businesses close for the whole week.
fact: The name comes from Feriae Augusti, a rest period introduced by Emperor Augustus in 18 BC.

clue: Yukon's Discovery Day recalls the 1896 find at Bonanza Creek
description: Gold was found on 16 August 1896, sparking a stampede to the Yukon. Discovery Day is the third Monday of August, which is 16 August itself in 2027.
fact: About 100,000 people set out for the Yukon, but only around 30,000 to 40,000 made it.

clue: Sisters tie a sacred thread on brothers' wrists in exchange for a promise of protection
description: This Hindu festival falls on the full moon of Shravana, which is 17 August in 2027. Sisters tie a rakhi and brothers give gifts in return.
fact: Its name means "bond of protection" in Sanskrit.

clue: An 1868 solar eclipse in India revealed a yellow line in the Sun's spectrum
description: On 18 August 1868 Jules Janssen observed a total solar eclipse in Guntur, India, and saw an unknown yellow line, later identified as a new element.
fact: It was found on the Sun before it was found on Earth, where it was isolated in 1895.

clue: Marks 1839, when France gave Daguerre's image process free to the world
description: World Photography Day marks 19 August 1839, when the French government announced the daguerreotype process as a gift to the world.
fact: The oldest surviving camera photograph, a view from a window by Niepce, dates from about 1827.

clue: Hungary honours its founding king with huge fireworks over the Danube
description: Hungary's national day on 20 August celebrates its first king, Stephen I, and the founding of the state, with fireworks in Budapest.
fact: His mummified right hand, the Holy Right, is carried in a procession through Budapest.

clue: Leonardo's portrait vanished from the Louvre in 1911 and was missing for two years
description: On 21 August 1911 the painting was stolen from the Louvre by Vincenzo Peruggia. The theft made it the world's most famous painting.
fact: The thief hid in a cupboard overnight and walked out with it under his smock.

clue: Chennai celebrates its 1639 founding, when land was bought for Fort St George
description: Chennai marks 22 August 1639, when the East India Company acquired the land where Fort St George and the city grew.
fact: The city was officially renamed Chennai in 1996.

clue: In 1989 about two million people held hands across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania
description: On 23 August 1989 around two million people formed a human chain through the three countries in a peaceful call for independence.
fact: The chain stretched about 675 km from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius.

clue: Kyiv marks its 1991 declaration of sovereignty from the Soviet Union
description: Ukraine's national day marks 24 August 1991, when its parliament declared the country's independence.
fact: The blue and yellow flag is often said to stand for a blue sky over golden wheat fields.

clue: Bunol near Valencia hosts an hour-long street fight with squashed red fruit
description: This messy festival is held on the last Wednesday of August, 25 August in 2027, in the town of Bunol.
fact: Since 2013 the event has been ticketed, with a cap of 20,000 participants.

clue: Born in Skopje in 1910, she founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata
description: The nun famous for her work with the poor in India was born on 26 August 1910 in Skopje, now in North Macedonia.
fact: She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and was declared a saint in 2016.

clue: Australian cricketer born in 1908 with a Test batting average of 99.94
description: Sir Donald Bradman, widely seen as the greatest batsman of all time, was born in Cootamundra, New South Wales, on 27 August 1908.
fact: He needed just four runs in his final Test innings to average 100, but was out for a duck.

clue: Martin Luther King Jr.'s 1963 speech at the Lincoln Memorial
description: On 28 August 1963 King delivered his speech to about 250,000 people at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.
fact: The famous passage was partly improvised after singer Mahalia Jackson called out "Tell them about the dream!"

clue: London's Caribbean street party with steel bands and costumes on bank holiday weekend
description: The carnival runs over the August bank holiday weekend: Sunday 29 August (family day) and Monday 30 August in 2027.
fact: It is one of Europe's biggest street festivals, with around a million visitors each year.

clue: Mary Shelley, born on this date in 1797, wrote this tale of a scientist's creature
description: Fans celebrate the gothic novel on 30 August, the birthday of its author Mary Shelley, born in London in 1797.
fact: She began writing it at 18 during a ghost-story contest with Lord Byron at Lake Geneva.

clue: Malaysia marks its 1957 independence from Britain with cries of "freedom!"
description: Malaysia's national day celebrates the independence of the Federation of Malaya on 31 August 1957.
fact: Tunku Abdul Rahman proclaimed independence by shouting the word seven times at Kuala Lumpur's stadium.

clue: Russian pupils bring flowers to their teachers on the first morning of the school year
description: In Russia and several other former Soviet countries, the school year starts on 1 September with ceremonies, flowers and a "first bell" for new pupils.
fact: At the ceremony an older pupil often carries a first-grader on their shoulder while she rings a hand bell.

clue: Ho Chi Minh read a declaration in Hanoi's Ba Dinh Square in 1945
description: The country's national day marks 2 September 1945, when Ho Chi Minh proclaimed independence in Hanoi.
fact: His declaration opened by quoting the US Declaration of Independence: "All men are created equal."

clue: Founded by a stonemason saint in 301, it claims to be the oldest surviving republic
description: The tiny state celebrates its founding on 3 September 301 by Saint Marinus, a stonemason who fled persecution to Mount Titano.
fact: It is entirely surrounded by Italy and has a population of only about 34,000.

clue: Hindus welcome the elephant-headed god with clay idols later immersed in water
description: This ten-day Hindu festival begins on the 4th day of Bhadrapada, 4 September in 2027, and ends with immersion processions on 14 September.
fact: In 1893 Bal Gangadhar Tilak turned the private household festival into a huge public celebration in Pune and Mumbai.

clue: Launched in 1977, this NASA probe is now the most distant human-made object
description: NASA launched the probe on 5 September 1977, 50 years ago in 2027. It visited Jupiter and Saturn and entered interstellar space in 2012.
fact: It carries a Golden Record with greetings in 55 languages, music and sounds of Earth.

clue: US and Canadian workers' holiday on the first Monday of September
description: The US and Canada honour workers on the first Monday of September, 6 September in 2027. It marks the unofficial end of summer.
fact: An old American fashion rule says you should not wear white after it.

clue: In 1927 Philo Farnsworth sent the first all-electronic image: a single straight line
description: On 7 September 1927, 100 years ago in 2027, 21-year-old Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first image with a fully electronic system in San Francisco.
fact: Farnsworth said he got the idea as a teenager while ploughing a potato field in neat rows.

clue: Gene Roddenberry's series about the starship Enterprise premiered on NBC in 1966
description: The original series premiered on NBC on 8 September 1966, now celebrated by fans as its anniversary day.
fact: Its very first broadcast was actually in Canada, on CTV, two days earlier.

clue: Russian author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina, born in 1828
description: The great novelist was born on 9 September 1828 at Yasnaya Polyana, his family estate south of Moscow.
fact: He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature several times but never won it.

clue: CERN's 27 km particle accelerator under Geneva circulated its first beam in 2008
description: On 10 September 2008 protons first circulated around the world's largest particle accelerator, on the French-Swiss border.
fact: In 2012 it found the Higgs boson, the particle linked to mass.

clue: Kerala's harvest festival with flower carpets, snake-boat races and a banana-leaf feast
description: Kerala's biggest festival peaks with First Onam on 11 September and Thiruvonam on 12 September 2027, welcoming the legendary King Mahabali.
fact: The festive meal, the sadya, can feature more than 20 dishes served on a banana leaf.

clue: Ethiopian New Year; in 2027 it falls a day late because 2028 is a leap year
description: Ethiopia's New Year is usually 11 September, but falls on 12 September in the year before a Gregorian leap year, as in 2027.
fact: Ethiopia's calendar runs about seven to eight years behind the Gregorian one, so the year 2020 begins now.

clue: Author of Matilda and The BFG, born in Wales in 1916
description: Fans celebrate the storyteller on his birthday, 13 September; he was born in Llandaff, Cardiff, in 1916.
fact: As a schoolboy he tested new chocolate bars for Cadbury, which inspired Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.

clue: Korean harvest holiday when families visit ancestral graves and eat songpyeon
description: Korea's three-day harvest holiday runs from 14 to 16 September 2027, centred on the 15th day of the 8th lunar month.
fact: Tens of millions of Koreans travel to their home towns, causing some of the year's worst traffic jams.

clue: Families share mooncakes and admire the full moon of the 8th lunar month
description: The festival falls on the 15th day of the 8th lunar month, 15 September in 2027, when the moon is said to be at its brightest.
fact: Legend says the goddess Chang'e lives on the Moon with a jade rabbit.

clue: Commemorates Father Hidalgo's 1810 Cry of Dolores, the start of the revolt
description: On 16 September 1810 priest Miguel Hidalgo called for revolt against Spain. The president repeats his cry from the National Palace the night before.
fact: The bell Hidalgo rang now hangs at the National Palace in Mexico City and is rung each 15 September.

clue: Medieval German abbess, composer, healer and mystic; feast day is 17 September
description: The 12th-century abbess died on 17 September 1179; her feast day honours a saint, composer and writer on medicine and nature.
fact: She is one of the earliest composers known by name, and even invented her own alphabet.

clue: Munich's mayor taps the first beer keg at noon, crying "O'zapft is!"
description: The world's biggest beer festival opens on Saturday 18 September and runs to 3 October 2027 on Munich's Theresienwiese.
fact: It began as the wedding celebration of Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese in October 1810.

clue: Arr, matey! Joke holiday invented by two friends in Oregon in 1995
description: Every 19 September, fans greet each other with "Ahoy!" and "Shiver me timbers!". Two friends made it up during a game of racquetball.
fact: It went global after humour columnist Dave Barry promoted it in 2002.

clue: In 1519 his five ships left Spain on the first voyage around the world
description: On 20 September 1519 the Portuguese navigator sailed from Sanlucar de Barrameda with five ships for the Spanish crown.
fact: Only one ship, the Victoria, and 18 men completed the voyage, returning in 1522.

clue: UN observance with a minute of silence at noon and a call for a global ceasefire
description: The UN's International Day of Peace has been held on 21 September since 2002, with a call for 24 hours of non-violence.
fact: The UN Peace Bell in New York was cast from coins donated by children from 60 countries.

clue: Bilbo and Frodo Baggins share their birthday on this date
description: Tolkien fans celebrate on 22 September, the shared birthday of Bilbo and Frodo Baggins in The Lord of the Rings.
fact: Tolkien wrote the book's famous first line on a blank page of an exam paper he was marking.

clue: Day and night are roughly the same length as fall begins in the north
description: The September equinox in 2027 falls on 23 September (06:01 UTC), when the Sun crosses the celestial equator and autumn begins in the north.
fact: Day and night are not exactly equal: refraction of sunlight makes daytime several minutes longer.

clue: South Africans mark their national heritage holiday by firing up the barbecue
description: South Africa's Heritage Day on 24 September is popularly celebrated with a braai, a barbecue that unites people of all cultures.
fact: Archbishop Desmond Tutu became patron of the initiative in 2008.

clue: In 1513 Balboa crossed Panama and became the first European to see this sea
description: On 25 September 1513 Vasco Nunez de Balboa sighted the great sea from a peak in Panama, calling it the "South Sea".
fact: Magellan later named it "peaceful" because the waters were calm when he crossed.

clue: Russian scientist born in 1849, famous for dogs drooling at the sound of a signal
description: Ivan Pavlov, the physiologist known for classical conditioning, was born in Ryazan on 26 September 1849.
fact: He won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his work on digestion, not for his conditioning experiments.

clue: The search giant celebrates its birthday with a special Doodle
description: The company celebrates its birthday on 27 September. It was founded by Larry Page and Sergey Brin in 1998.
fact: Its name comes from "googol", the number 1 followed by 100 zeros.

clue: Alexander Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria in a petri dish in 1928
description: On 28 September 1928 Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to his London lab and noticed mould killing bacteria, leading to the first antibiotic.
fact: The mould got in because Fleming had left his lab untidy, with dishes stacked on a bench.

clue: Italian physicist born in Rome in 1901 who built the first nuclear reactor
description: The Nobel-winning physicist was born in Rome on 29 September 1901.
fact: Element 100, fermium, is named after him.

clue: Mozart's opera featuring a Queen of Night aria premiered in Vienna in 1791
description: Mozart's last opera premiered in Vienna on 30 September 1791, with the composer conducting.
fact: Librettist Emanuel Schikaneder played the bird-catcher Papageno himself at the premiere.

clue: Australia hosts the oval-ball tournament, opening in Perth with 24 teams
description: The 2027 men's tournament opens on 1 October in Perth, with Australia playing Hong Kong; the final is in Sydney on 13 November.
fact: The trophy is the Webb Ellis Cup, named after the schoolboy said to have invented the game.

clue: Jewish New Year 5788, greeted with a ram's horn and apples dipped in honey
description: The Jewish New Year begins at sundown on 1 October 2027, with 2 and 3 October as its two days. It starts the year 5788.
fact: Its name means "head of the year"; round challah bread is eaten to symbolise the cycle of the year.

clue: Marks the 1990 reunification of East and West, 11 months after the Wall fell
description: Germany's national day celebrates 3 October 1990, when the German Democratic Republic joined the Federal Republic.
fact: It is the only national holiday set by federal law in Germany; other holidays are set by the states.

clue: Soviet beach-ball-sized satellite that started the Space Age in 1957
description: The Soviet Union launched the first artificial satellite on 4 October 1957, 70 years ago in 2027, starting the space race.
fact: Its radio beeps could be picked up by amateur radio operators around the world.

clue: UNESCO honours educators, marking a 1966 recommendation on their status
description: World Teachers' Day on 5 October, held since 1994, honours educators everywhere and marks a 1966 UNESCO and ILO recommendation.
fact: Many countries keep their own dates: India celebrates on 5 September and China on 10 September.

clue: Al Jolson's 1927 film, first feature with synchronised spoken lines
description: The first feature film with synchronised dialogue premiered in New York on 6 October 1927, 100 years ago in 2027, ending the silent era.
fact: Its first spoken words were "Wait a minute, wait a minute, you ain't heard nothin' yet!"

clue: Luna 3 photographed a lunar hemisphere never visible from Earth in 1959
description: On 7 October 1959 the Soviet probe Luna 3 took the first photographs of the half of the Moon that always faces away from Earth.
fact: Despite the nickname "dark side", it gets just as much sunlight as the near side.

clue: Percy Spencer filed a patent after a chocolate bar melted in his pocket near radar
description: On 8 October 1945 engineer Percy Spencer filed a patent for cooking with radio waves, after noticing radar equipment heating food.
fact: The first commercial model, the Radarange, stood almost 1.8 m tall.

clue: Hindus burn giant effigies of Ravana to mark good triumphing over evil
description: Also called Vijayadashami, it falls on the 10th day of Ashvin, 9 October in 2027, ending the Navratri festival.
fact: Mysore's celebration features a grand procession with decorated elephants.

clue: Taiwan celebrates the 1911 Wuchang Uprising on the 10th of the 10th month
description: Taiwan's national day marks the Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911, which led to the end of imperial rule in China.
fact: Celebrations include a parade and fireworks in front of the Presidential Office in Taipei.

clue: Families gather for turkey and pumpkin pie on the second Monday of October
description: In Canada the harvest holiday falls on the second Monday of October, 11 October in 2027.
fact: It is often linked to explorer Martin Frobisher's 1578 feast in the Arctic, decades before the Pilgrims.

clue: Celebrates women in science, named after the first computer programmer
description: Held on the second Tuesday of October (12 October in 2027), it celebrates women in science, technology, engineering and maths.
fact: In 1843 she published what is considered the first computer program, for Babbage's Analytical Engine.

clue: In 1884 delegates in Washington chose Greenwich as zero degrees longitude
description: On 13 October 1884 the International Meridian Conference in Washington voted for the line through Greenwich as the world's zero of longitude.
fact: France abstained and kept using the Paris meridian on its maps for decades.

clue: Chuck Yeager flew the Bell X-1 faster than Mach 1 in 1947
description: On 14 October 1947, 80 years ago in 2027, Chuck Yeager became the first pilot to fly faster than sound in level flight.
fact: He flew with two broken ribs from a horse-riding accident and named the plane Glamorous Glennis after his wife.

clue: German philosopher born in 1844 who wrote "God is dead" and Thus Spoke Zarathustra
description: The philosopher was born in Rocken, near Leipzig, on 15 October 1844.
fact: He became a professor at Basel at just 24, before he had even finished his doctorate.

clue: Jewish harvest festival of eating meals in temporary huts with leafy roofs
description: This week-long festival begins at sundown on 15 October 2027, with 16 October as its first full day.
fact: The roof of the hut must be thin enough to see the stars through it.

clue: His company opened the first regular radio service across the Atlantic in 1907
description: On 17 October 1907 the radio pioneer's company began regular transatlantic wireless service between Clifden, Ireland, and Glace Bay, Canada.
fact: He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Karl Ferdinand Braun.

clue: Founded in 1922, the broadcaster Brits call "the Beeb" or "Auntie"
description: The British Broadcasting Company was formed on 18 October 1922; it became a public corporation in 1927.
fact: Its first director-general, John Reith, set its mission: to inform, educate and entertain.

clue: Brazilian aviator who flew his airship around the Eiffel Tower in 1901
description: On 19 October 1901 Alberto Santos-Dumont flew his airship No. 6 around the Eiffel Tower and back to win the Deutsch Prize.
fact: He helped popularise the wristwatch: Cartier made one so he could keep his hands on the controls.

clue: Queen Elizabeth II opened Jorn Utzon's sail-roofed harbour icon in 1973
description: The performing arts centre was opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 20 October 1973 and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
fact: Architect Jorn Utzon left the project in 1966 and never saw the finished building.

clue: Edison's carbon-filament lamp glowed for over 13 hours in an 1879 test
description: On 21 October 1879 Thomas Edison's team tested a carbon-filament lamp that glowed for more than 13 hours.
fact: Edison later found that carbonised bamboo filaments could last over 1,200 hours.

clue: In 1797 Andre-Jacques Garnerin jumped from a hydrogen balloon over Paris
description: On 22 October 1797 Garnerin made the first frameless silk jump from about 900 m above Parc Monceau in Paris.
fact: His canopy had no vent, so it swung wildly and he was sick on the way down.

clue: Chemists celebrate Avogadro's number from 6:02 a.m. to 6:02 p.m. on 10/23
description: Chemistry fans celebrate on 23 October from 6:02 to 6:02, echoing Avogadro's number, 6.02 x 10^23.
fact: Since 2019 the number has been fixed exactly at 6.02214076 x 10^23.

clue: Marks the 1945 entry into force of the organisation's Charter
description: The world body's founding Charter came into force on 24 October 1945, after ratification by most signatories.
fact: It started with 51 member states; today it has 193.

clue: Italy's beloved durum wheat staple, from spaghetti to penne
description: Launched in 1998 at the first World Pasta Congress in Rome, the day on 25 October celebrates Italy's favourite food.
fact: Italians eat about 23 kg of it per person each year, more than any other nation.

clue: Vienna marks the 1955 law on permanent neutrality with open state buildings
description: Austria's national day marks 26 October 1955, when parliament passed its Declaration of Neutrality.
fact: The army holds a show on Heldenplatz and government buildings open their doors to visitors.

clue: Genoese violin virtuoso born in 1782, rumoured to have sold his soul for his skill
description: The legendary violinist and composer Niccolo Paganini was born in Genoa on 27 October 1782.
fact: His playing was so astonishing that rumours said he had made a pact with the devil.

clue: A gift from France, dedicated in New York Harbor in 1886
description: The colossal copper statue designed by Bartholdi was dedicated on 28 October 1886 on Bedloe's Island in New York Harbor.
fact: Its copper skin is only about 2.4 mm thick.

clue: Rows of oil lamps light up homes for the festival of lights
description: The Hindu festival of lights centres on Lakshmi Puja on the new moon of Kartika, 29 October in 2027.
fact: It is also a public holiday in Nepal, Fiji, Mauritius, Singapore and Trinidad and Tobago.

clue: Orson Welles's 1938 radio play about Martians invading New Jersey
description: On 30 October 1938 Orson Welles broadcast a radio adaptation of H.G. Wells's novel, presented as live news bulletins.
fact: Stories of mass panic were greatly exaggerated by newspapers keen to discredit radio.

clue: Costumes, carved pumpkins and trick-or-treating on the eve of All Saints
description: Celebrated on 31 October, the eve of All Hallows (All Saints), it grew from the Celtic festival of Samhain.
fact: The first jack-o'-lanterns in Ireland and Scotland were carved from turnips.

clue: Christian feast honouring every holy person, known or unknown
description: On 1 November Christians honour all the saints. It is a public holiday in much of Europe and Latin America.
fact: In Poland millions visit cemeteries to light candles, making graveyards glow at night.

clue: Mexican families build altars with marigolds and sugar skulls for loved ones
description: Dia de Muertos (1-2 November) is a joyful festival where families welcome the spirits of their relatives with altars, food and music.
fact: UNESCO added it to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2008.

clue: Japanese holiday with arts festivals and imperial awards, on Emperor Meiji's birthday
description: Japan's 3 November holiday promotes freedom, peace and the arts. It falls on the birthday of Emperor Meiji.
fact: The Order of Culture, one of Japan's highest honours, is presented by the Emperor on this day.

clue: UN agency based in Paris that keeps the World Heritage List
description: The UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization's constitution came into force on 4 November 1946; its headquarters are in Paris.
fact: Its World Heritage List now includes more than 1,200 sites.

clue: Fireworks recall Guy Fawkes and the failed 1605 plot to blow up Parliament
description: On 5 November Britain lights fires and fireworks to mark the foiling of the Gunpowder Plot in 1605.
fact: Before every State Opening of Parliament, the Yeomen of the Guard still search the cellars.

clue: Canadian-born teacher, born in 1861, who invented basketball with peach baskets
description: The inventor of basketball was born in Almonte, Ontario, on 6 November 1861. He devised the game in 1891 at a college in Springfield, Massachusetts.
fact: The first game ever played ended 1-0.

clue: Author of The Stranger, born in French Algeria in 1913
description: The writer and philosopher was born in Mondovi (now Dréan), Algeria, on 7 November 1913.
fact: At 44 he became one of the youngest winners of the Nobel Prize in Literature.

clue: Wilhelm Rontgen found this invisible radiation in 1895 and imaged his wife's hand
description: On 8 November 1895 Wilhelm Rontgen discovered a new kind of radiation in his lab in Wurzburg, Germany.
fact: He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 and refused to patent his discovery.

clue: Hollywood star born in Vienna in 1914 who co-invented frequency hopping
description: The actress and inventor was born in Vienna on 9 November 1914. Her radio frequency-hopping idea fed into later wireless technology.
fact: Germany, Austria and Switzerland celebrate Inventors' Day on her birthday.

clue: In 1871 Stanley found the Scottish missionary at Ujiji: "Dr ..., I presume?"
description: On 10 November 1871 journalist Henry Morton Stanley found the missing explorer at Ujiji, on Lake Tanganyika in present-day Tanzania.
fact: Stanley had been sent by the New York Herald and spent about eight months searching.

clue: Children carry paper lanterns and sing door to door for sweets on 11 November
description: On the feast of Saint Martin of Tours, children in the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium walk with lanterns, and many families eat goose.
fact: The saint is said to have cut his cloak in half to share it with a freezing beggar.

clue: Born in 1866, he is called the father of modern China
description: The revolutionary leader and first president of the Republic of China was born on 12 November 1866. Taiwan marks the day as a national holiday.
fact: His name is honoured in both mainland China and Taiwan, a rare point of agreement.

clue: Thais float candlelit lotus-shaped baskets on rivers under the full moon
description: This festival falls on the full moon of the 12th Thai lunar month, 13 November in 2027.
fact: In Chiang Mai, the Yi Peng festival releases thousands of sky lanterns at the same time.

clue: Sikhs celebrate their founder's birth with processions and free community kitchens
description: Sikhs celebrate their founder's birth on the full moon of Kartik, 14 November in 2027.
fact: The free kitchen at Amritsar's Golden Temple can serve up to 100,000 meals a day.

clue: Intel advertised the 4004, the first commercial computer-on-a-chip, in 1971
description: Intel announced the 4004, the first commercially available chip of its kind, on 15 November 1971.
fact: It had about 2,300 transistors; today's chips have billions.

clue: Nigerian author of Things Fall Apart, born in 1930
description: The Nigerian novelist, often called the father of modern African literature, was born in Ogidi on 16 November 1930.
fact: Things Fall Apart has sold over 20 million copies and been translated into more than 50 languages.

clue: Student protests in Prague in 1989 peacefully ended communist rule
description: A student march in Prague on 17 November 1989 sparked the peaceful protests that ended one-party rule in Czechoslovakia.
fact: Playwright Vaclav Havel became president just six weeks later.

clue: Riga marks the 1918 founding of the republic with fireworks over the Daugava
description: Latvia's national day marks 18 November 1918, when the Republic of Latvia was proclaimed in Riga.
fact: Many Latvians wear a small red-white-red ribbon pinned to their clothes in November.

clue: The principality on the Riviera fetes its prince with a Mass and fireworks
description: The Fete du Prince on 19 November honours the reigning prince, with celebrations around the palace.
fact: At about 2 square kilometres, it is the world's second-smallest country.

clue: Microsoft's first graphical operating system shipped as version 1.0 in 1985
description: Microsoft released its first graphical operating environment on 20 November 1985.
fact: In version 1.0 the program windows could not overlap; they could only be tiled side by side.

clue: Belgian surrealist born in 1898 who painted a pipe captioned "This is not a pipe"
description: The Belgian surrealist painter was born in Lessines on 21 November 1898.
fact: Before his art took off, he earned a living designing wallpaper and advertising posters.

clue: Beirut marks the 1943 end of the French mandate with a parade
description: Lebanon's national day marks 22 November 1943, when the French mandate ended.
fact: The cedar tree on the flag is mentioned dozens of times in the Bible.

clue: Written 11/23, it spells 1, 1, 2, 3, the start of a famous sequence from Pisa
description: Maths fans celebrate on 23 November because 11/23 gives the first numbers of the sequence popularised by Leonardo of Pisa in 1202.
fact: Dividing each number by the one before it gets ever closer to the golden ratio, about 1.618.

clue: Darwin's 1859 book on natural selection sold out on its first day
description: Charles Darwin's book on evolution by natural selection was published on 24 November 1859, now marked as Evolution Day.
fact: The word "evolution" never appears in the first edition; only "evolved", as its last word.

clue: Americans eat turkey and watch parades on the fourth Thursday of November
description: The US holiday falls on the fourth Thursday of November, 25 November in 2027.
fact: The Macy's parade in New York has been held since 1924.

clue: Lewis Carroll's 1865 tale of a girl who falls down a rabbit hole
description: Lewis Carroll's classic was published by Macmillan on 26 November 1865.
fact: Carroll first told the story to Alice Liddell and her sisters on a boat trip in 1862.

clue: Martial arts film star born in 1940, famous for Enter the Dragon
description: The martial artist and actor, raised in Hong Kong, was born on 27 November 1940.
fact: He was born in San Francisco's Chinatown in both the hour and the year of the Dragon.

clue: Suffragist whose petitions won women the vote; they first used it on 28 November 1893
description: On 28 November 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country where women voted in a general election, thanks to the campaign led by this suffragist.
fact: Kate Sheppard, who led the campaign, appears on New Zealand's $10 note.

clue: Atari's 1972 arcade table-tennis game with two paddles and a dot
description: Atari released its arcade table-tennis game on 29 November 1972, launching the video game industry.
fact: Its prototype in a California bar stopped working because the coin box was overflowing.

clue: Scotland's patron, whose X-shaped cross forms the Saltire flag
description: Scotland celebrates its patron on 30 November with ceilidhs, music and food.
fact: He is also the patron of Greece, Romania, Russia and Ukraine.

clue: Romania marks Transylvania's 1918 joining with the kingdom
description: Romania's national day marks 1 December 1918, when an assembly at Alba Iulia voted to unite Transylvania with Romania.
fact: Bucharest holds a parade under its Arcul de Triumf, modelled on the one in Paris.

clue: Opera soprano born in New York in 1923 to Greek parents, nicknamed La Divina
description: The legendary Greek soprano was born in New York on 2 December 1923.
fact: Angelina Jolie played her in the 2024 film Maria.

clue: Polish-born author of Heart of Darkness, born in 1857, who wrote in English
description: The novelist was born Jozef Korzeniowski in Berdychiv (then Poland, now Ukraine) on 3 December 1857.
fact: He only became fluent in English in his twenties, after years as a merchant seaman.

clue: On her feast, cherry twigs are cut to bloom by Christmas; patron of miners
description: Her feast day is 4 December. In Germany and Austria, people cut cherry branches that should blossom by Christmas.
fact: She is the patron of miners, artillerymen and firefighters because of the lightning in her legend.

clue: Furry horned monsters roam Alpine towns to scare naughty children
description: On the eve of St Nicholas's Day, men in fur and carved masks parade through Austrian and Bavarian towns.
fact: The name comes from the old German word Krampen, meaning claw.

clue: Children leave shoes out overnight for treats from the bishop of Myra
description: On 6 December many European children find sweets in their shoes or boots, left by the generous 4th-century bishop.
fact: His relics have been in Bari, Italy, since sailors took them there in 1087.

clue: Milan's opera house opens its season on Saint Ambrose's day
description: The famous Milan opera house opens its season on 7 December, the feast of the city's patron, Saint Ambrose.
fact: It opened in 1778 with Antonio Salieri's opera Europa riconosciuta.

clue: Buddhists mark the Buddha's enlightenment under a fig tree; Japan's Rohatsu
description: Many Mahayana Buddhists, especially in Japan, celebrate the Buddha's enlightenment on 8 December.
fact: Zen monasteries hold an intense week-long meditation retreat leading up to it.

clue: Born in 1906, the US Navy rear admiral who helped create COBOL
description: The computer pioneer and US Navy rear admiral was born in New York on 9 December 1906.
fact: She popularised the term "debugging" after a moth was found in a computer in 1947.

clue: Marks the UN's 1948 adoption of the Universal Declaration in Paris
description: The UN General Assembly adopted its landmark declaration in Paris on 10 December 1948.
fact: The declaration is one of the world's most translated documents, in over 500 languages.

clue: Cairo novelist born in 1911, the first Arabic-language Nobel literature laureate
description: The Egyptian novelist was born in Cairo on 11 December 1911 and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988.
fact: His Cairo Trilogy follows three generations of one family through the city's changing streets.

clue: Norwegian painter born in 1863, creator of The Scream
description: The expressionist painter was born on 12 December 1863 in Loten, Norway.
fact: He made several versions of The Scream, in paint, pastel and print.

clue: Dutch navigator who in 1642 became the first European to sight New Zealand
description: On 13 December 1642 the Dutch explorer's ships sighted the west coast of New Zealand's South Island.
fact: Tasmania and the Tasman Sea are named after him.

clue: Danish astronomer born in 1546 who wore a metal nose after a duel
description: The Danish astronomer famous for precise naked-eye observations was born on 14 December 1546 in Scania.
fact: His careful records let his assistant Kepler work out the laws of planetary motion.

clue: Soviet probe that made the first soft landing on Venus in 1970
description: On 15 December 1970 the Soviet probe became the first spacecraft to transmit data from the surface of another planet.
fact: It kept sending signals for about 23 minutes in heat of around 475 C.

clue: Author of Pride and Prejudice, born in Hampshire in 1775
description: The novelist was born in Steventon, Hampshire, on 16 December 1775.
fact: Her novels were published anonymously during her lifetime; her first was credited "By a Lady".

clue: Ancient Roman winter festival of feasting, gifts and role reversal starting 17 December
description: Romans held this festival for the god Saturn from 17 December, with banquets, gift-giving and masters serving their slaves.
fact: Romans greeted each other with "Io Saturnalia!" and swapped togas for colourful party clothes.

clue: Tchaikovsky's Christmas ballet premiered at St Petersburg's Mariinsky in 1892
description: Tchaikovsky's ballet premiered at the Mariinsky Theatre in St Petersburg on 18 December 1892.
fact: It was not a hit at first; it became a Christmas tradition in the US from the 1950s.

clue: Paris "little sparrow" born in 1915 who sang La Vie en rose
description: The French singer of La Vie en rose and Non, je ne regrette rien was born in Paris on 19 December 1915.
fact: Her stage name comes from Parisian slang for "sparrow".

clue: Portugal returned this Chinese enclave in 1999, ending over four centuries of rule
description: On 20 December 1999 Portugal handed the territory back to China; the anniversary is a public holiday there.
fact: It is the only part of China where casino gambling is legal.

clue: Arthur Wynne's diamond-shaped puzzle grid appeared in a New York paper in 1913
description: The first puzzle of this kind, by Arthur Wynne, appeared in the New York World on 21 December 1913.
fact: The New York Times resisted the craze for decades, only launching its own in 1942.

clue: Self-taught Indian maths genius born in 1887; 1729 is his taxicab number
description: The self-taught mathematician was born in Erode on 22 December 1887. India celebrates National Mathematics Day on his birthday.
fact: When Hardy called 1729 a dull taxi number, he replied it is the smallest sum of two cubes in two different ways.

clue: French scholar born in 1790 who decoded Egyptian hieroglyphs using the Rosetta Stone
description: Jean-Francois Champollion, the founder of Egyptology, was born in Figeac on 23 December 1790.
fact: Legend says that after his breakthrough in 1822 he cried "I've got it!" and fainted.

clue: A night of carols, midnight Mass and stockings hung for Santa
description: The evening before Christmas Day is celebrated with church services, family dinners and, in many countries, gift-giving.
fact: In Germany and Scandinavia, presents are traditionally opened on this evening rather than the next morning.

clue: Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus with gifts and family feasts
description: Christmas is celebrated on 25 December by most Christians, with gifts, carols and festive meals.
fact: In Japan, fried chicken is a popular festive dinner thanks to a 1974 KFC marketing campaign.

clue: Bahamian street parade with cowbells, goatskin drums and crepe-paper costumes
description: The Bahamas' biggest festival takes over Nassau's Bay Street in the early hours of 26 December and again on New Year's Day.
fact: Groups spend months building their costumes, and parades start around 2 a.m.

clue: Jewish festival of lights: one more candle is lit on the menorah each night
description: The eight-day festival begins at sundown on 24 December 2027 and lasts until 1 January 2028.
fact: Jelly doughnuts called sufganiyot are eaten because they are fried in oil, recalling the miracle of the oil.

clue: Finnish programmer born in 1969 who created a famous open-source kernel and Git
description: The creator of the Linux operating system kernel was born in Helsinki on 28 December 1969.
fact: Linux's penguin mascot, Tux, was chosen partly because he says he was once bitten by a penguin.

clue: African American week-long festival of seven principles and a seven-candle kinara
description: This celebration of African heritage runs from 26 December to 1 January, with one principle for each day.
fact: Created in 1966 by Maulana Karenga, its name comes from a Swahili phrase meaning "first fruits".

clue: Asia's first underground railway opened between Ueno and Asakusa in 1927
description: Asia's first subway line opened on 30 December 1927 in Japan's capital, 100 years ago in 2027; today it is the Ginza Line.
fact: The first line ran just 2.2 km between Asakusa and Ueno.

clue: Scotland's New Year's Eve, with Auld Lang Syne and first-footing
description: Scots see in the New Year with street parties, fireworks and the singing of Robert Burns's Auld Lang Syne.
fact: First-footing: the first visitor after midnight should bring coal, shortbread or whisky for good luck.
